related_questions.question: What are the risk factors for the development of asthma?

text_blocks.snippet: Several risk factors can increase the likelihood of developing asthma, including genetic predisposition, allergies, exposure to certain environmental factors, and lifestyle choices.
snippet_highlighted_words: genetic predisposition, allergies, exposure to certain environmental factors, and lifestyle choices

list.snippet: Family History: Having a parent or sibling with asthma significantly increases the risk.
Atopy: Individuals with other allergic conditions like eczema or hay fever (allergic rhinitis) are more prone to developing asthma.

list.title: Air Pollution:
list.snippet: Exposure to traffic-related air pollution, and other pollutants like particulate matter (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and black carbon, can increase the risk of asthma development and worsen symptoms, according to ATS Journals.

list.title: Occupational Exposures:
list.snippet: Certain chemicals and industrial dusts in the workplace can trigger asthma, known as occupational asthma.

list.title: Tobacco Smoke:
list.snippet: Exposure to tobacco smoke, both during pregnancy and in early childhood, is a significant risk factor.

list.title: Infections:
list.snippet: Severe respiratory infections in early childhood, especially those causing wheezing, can predispose individuals to asthma later in life.

list.title: Early Life Exposures:
list.snippet: Low socioeconomic status and medication exposure in early life have also been associated with asthma development.

list.title: Obesity:
list.snippet: Being overweight or obese is linked to an increased risk of asthma, especially in children and adolescents, according to Banner Health.

list.title: Smoking:
list.snippet: Smoking, including e-cigarettes, can increase the risk of asthma, especially in adolescents and adults.

list.title: Low Physical Activity:
list.snippet: A lack of physical activity is also associated with a higher risk of asthma, according to ATS Journals.
Male Sex: Asthma is more common in boys during childhood, but more common in women in adulthood.
Race and Ethnicity: Certain racial and ethnic groups, such as Black or Puerto Rican individuals, have a higher risk of asthma.
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD): GERD can be a contributing factor to asthma symptoms.
